When I was twenty-four, I lived in one room in a Mumbai chawl with two other boys. Shared toilet, a tin trunk for a cupboard. I worked in a printing press all day. I wanted to write poems.

Well, I'm learning to. I apprentice with an old craftsman in Thanjavur. Wood shavings in my hair, glue on my fingers, and I've never been happier.

Hafsa, your Ammi says you've been at the mall every evening. Let me tell you about the boy I was at fifteen.
In old Hyderabad, I lived for fun. Cricket in the lane till dark. Irani chai and Osmania biscuits at the café with my gang. Every new film on the first day, even if I had to sell my comics for the ticket.

That summer, I kept the cricket, but I made a rule: two hours of maths first, then the lane. I passed in the supplementary exam.
I'm Santosh, beta. Keep the fun. Just don't let it hold the steering wheel.

Vijay, you asked on this podcast how I think about pleasure. I'm Manjula, I'm twenty-six, and I have a mango rule.
In summer, I eat one Alphonso mango every evening. Standing at the sink, juice running down my arms, no phone, no TV. Ten whole minutes. It's the best part of my day.
I don't eat five. I tried that once. By the fourth, I couldn't taste anything.
That's how I try to do everything. Real lunch breaks. A nap on Sundays. Dancing at weddings until my feet hurt. I think joy is serious business.
But I don't chase the next thrill. I don't need a bigger party every weekend. I need to actually be at the one I'm at.
And I still go to work, pay my bills and see my doctor when I should. The mango doesn't replace those. It just makes them bearable.
